## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Present Simple, Present Continuous and State Verbs
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Ingrid usually starts the day by reading the news from five countries. Tomás writes articles and often interviews people. Aisha takes photographs, and she always asks for consent first. These are the things that the team does every day. But today is different. Right now, the whole team is preparing the winter campaign. Nadia is writing posts, Aisha is choosing photographs, and Joseph is talking to families in Nairobi. Notice the difference: we use the present simple for routines and facts, and the present continuous for actions that are happening now.

**Look at the verbs in your teacher’s copy. Which verbs describe a routine? Which describe an action happening now?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Present simple | Aisha always asks for consent. | routines, facts, and frequency |  |
| Present continuous | Right now, she is choosing photographs. | actions happening now or these days |  |
| State verbs | I know the answer. (not ‘I am knowing’) | feelings and states, not usually continuous |  |
| Adverbs of frequency | always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never | before the main verb; after the verb ‘be’ |  |

**Remember:** Use the present simple for routines and facts, and the present continuous for actions happening now. State verbs (know, believe, need, want, prefer) are not usually used in the continuous.

**Watch out!** Watch out: put the adverb of frequency before the main verb (‘she often writes’) but after the verb ‘be’ (‘she is often busy’).

**Gloss:** fact = something that is always true    ·    temporary = lasting for a short time, not permanent

### Part 3: Ingrid Introduces the Team
**🔊 Audio Track 1.2**

*Before you listen: what different jobs do you think a communications team has?*

> Ingrid: Welcome to the communications team at Meridian Relief. Let me tell you what we do here. We are a small team in six places, but we work on many things at the same time. I usually start the day by checking the news and planning our posts. Tomás writes articles and interviews people from our office in Lima, and he is very good at asking the right questions. Aisha is our photographer in Freetown; she always asks for consent before she takes a picture. Nadia manages our social media from Dhaka, and at the moment she is preparing a big winter campaign. We do not just share information — we tell people’s stories with respect. That is the most important part of our job. Every day is different, and every day is busy, but I love this work, because it helps real families.

### Part 3: Tomás Asks for Advice
**🔊 Audio Track 1.3**

*Before you listen: when you are not sure about something at work, who do you ask?*

> Tomás: Ingrid, I am writing the post about the winter campaign. Can I ask you something?  
> Ingrid: Of course, Tomás. What is it?  
> Tomás: I have a lovely photo of a family, but I am not sure about the caption. What should I write?  
> Ingrid: Good question. First, always check that we have consent for the photo. Do we have it?  
> Tomás: Yes, the family signed the form yesterday, and Joseph translated it for them.  
> Ingrid: Perfect. Then keep the caption simple and true. Say who the family is — with their permission — and explain what we are doing to help.  
> Tomás: Should I include their address?  
> Ingrid: No, never. We always protect people’s privacy. The name of the town is enough.  
> Tomás: That makes sense. Thank you, Ingrid.  
> Ingrid: You are welcome. Remember, a good caption tells the truth and respects the person.

*While you listen: answer the questions. (0. is done.)*

0. What is Tomás writing? — A post about the winter campaign.

1. What must the team always check before they use a photo?
2. Did the family sign the consent form?
3. Should Tomás include the family’s address in the caption?

**Useful phrases:** Can I ask you something?  ·  Always check that…  ·  We protect people’s privacy.


### Part 3: Planning the Day
**🔊 Audio Track 1.4**

*Before you listen: how does a team decide who does each task?*

> Ingrid: Right, everyone, let’s plan today. We have a lot to do for the winter campaign. Tomás, you are writing the main article, so please focus on that this morning. Aisha, we need new photographs of the distribution centre — can you go there today?  
> Aisha: Yes, of course. I will take the camera.  
> Ingrid: Great. Nadia, you are managing the social media, so please prepare the posts for this week. And Joseph, I need you on the ground: talk to the families, with their consent, and collect their stories.  
> Joseph: Understood. I will be careful and respectful.  
> Ingrid: Thank you, everyone. Remember, we are one team in six places, and we always support each other. Let’s make this a good campaign.

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: What a Communications Team Does
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> The communications team at Meridian Relief has an important job: it helps the public understand the work of the organisation. The team does many different things. Writers prepare posts and short articles, photographers take pictures of the projects, and social media officers share the news online. Although the tasks are different, and although the team sits in six different cities, they all have the same goal — to tell true stories with respect. Every morning, the team meets online to plan the day. They decide which stories to tell and which photographs to use. Usually, they work on several projects at the same time. This week, for example, they are preparing a campaign about winter aid, because thousands of families need warm clothes and heating. Good communication is not easy. The team must think carefully about every word and every image, and about how each one will be read in a different country. They always ask for consent before they publish a photograph, and they never share private information. When people trust an organisation, they are more likely to support it. For this reason, honesty is the most valuable tool the team has. The work is demanding, but it is also rewarding. At the end of a long day, the team knows that its words have helped real people, and that is why they do this job.

### Part 5: Telling the Story from Where You Are
**Read about communication across countries. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> For many years, people in one part of the world have heard about another part mainly through difficult news. However, there is always much more to a country than its hardest years. Every country has a rich culture, a long history, and — most importantly — people who are working hard to rebuild their communities. Communicators in international organisations have a special responsibility. They want to show the real lives of the people they work with: their courage, their kindness, and their hope for the future. At the same time, they must always protect the people in their stories. They ask for consent, they respect privacy, and they never show anyone in a way that takes away their dignity. This is not always easy. Sometimes a powerful photograph could attract more attention, but if it harms a person, a good communicator will not use it. Wherever trust matters, honest and respectful communication is the only way to work. When the world hears true and dignified stories, it understands a place better, and it is more ready to help.

## Part 6  ·  Writing
*[OP] Officer track  ·  writing*


### Part 6: Describe Your Working Day (80–120 words)
**Describe a normal day in a communications job. Use the present simple, adverbs of frequency, and at least one present continuous sentence about this week.**

**Model — read this first:**

> I work as a media officer at an international humanitarian organisation. My days are busy, but I enjoy them. Every morning, I usually check the news and read the messages that arrived while my colleagues in other time zones were working. Then I meet my team online, and together we plan the stories that we want to tell. During the day, I often write posts and articles, and I always ask for consent before I use a photograph. This week, we are preparing a winter campaign, so at the moment I am writing about the families that we are helping. I love this work, because it helps real people.

**Plan (make notes, then write):** I work as…  Every morning, I usually…  I often…  I always…  This week, I am…  I enjoy this work because…

**Check before you finish:** ☐ present simple + adverbs of frequency?  ☐ one present continuous sentence?  ☐ 80–120 words?


### Part 6: Why Consent Matters (80–120 words)
**Write about why communicators must always ask for consent. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> Consent is one of the most important rules in communication. When we ask for consent, we show respect for the people in our stories. We also protect them, because a photograph or a name can put someone at risk. For example, if we share a family’s address without asking, we could put that family in danger. Some people think that a strong photo is more important than a rule, but they are wrong. A story that harms a person is never a good story. For this reason, a responsible communicator always asks first, and never publishes without permission.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear opinion?  ☐ two or three reasons?  ☐ one example?  ☐ 80–120 words?


### Part 6: A Short Message to a Colleague (60–90 words)
**Write a short message to a colleague about a post you are working on. Ask for their advice.**

**Model — read this first:**

> Hi Nadia, I am writing the post about the winter campaign, and I would like your advice. I have a lovely photo of a family, and they have given consent for it. However, I am not sure about the caption. Should I include the name of the town, or is that too much? I always want to protect people’s privacy, so I would rather ask you first. Could we talk about it this afternoon? Thank you, Tomás.

**Plan (make notes, then write):** Hi ___ ,  I am ___  and I would like ___ .  I am not sure about ___ .  Could we ___ ?  Thank you, ___ .

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a greeting and a close?  ☐ a clear request for advice?  ☐ 60–90 words?


### Part 6: Reflection — Why This Work Matters (60–90 words)
**Write about why communication work matters, especially between countries. Use your own ideas.**

**Model — read this first:**

> I believe that communication work matters, especially between countries that know little about each other. For many years, people abroad have heard only difficult news about places like mine. Good communicators can change this. They show the courage and the kindness of ordinary people, and they tell true stories with respect. When the world hears these stories, it understands us better, and it is more ready to help. This is why I think that honest, respectful communication is not a small job — it is an important one.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear main idea?  ☐ reasons or examples?  ☐ 60–90 words?

### 7B: The Manager’s Briefing
**🔊 Audio Track 1.5**

*Before you listen: what values do you think are important in a communications team?*

> Ingrid: Good morning, everyone, in all five offices. Before we start, I want to talk about how we work as a team. Communication is not only about writing well; it is about working together and following our values. First, we always tell the truth. We never exaggerate, and we never share information that we have not checked. Second, we always respect the people in our stories. We ask for consent, we protect privacy, and we treat everyone with dignity. Third, we help each other. If you are not sure about something, please ask. It is always better to ask than to make a mistake. This week, we are working on the winter campaign, and it is important that our message is clear, true and kind in every language we publish in. I know that you are all busy, but I also know that you are a wonderful team. Let’s do this work well, and let’s do it together.

### Part 8: Reading — A Day in the Life of Nadia
*Before you read: what do you think a social media officer does every day?*

> Nadia is a social media officer at Meridian Relief in Dhaka, and she loves her job. Her main task is to share the organisation’s news with the public. Every morning, she checks the messages that arrived overnight from colleagues in other time zones and answers people’s questions. She usually spends the first hour reading the news, because she needs to understand what is happening in the countries where Meridian Relief works. Nadia does not work alone. She is part of a team in six cities, and they often plan campaigns together. At the moment, she is helping to prepare the winter appeal. This week, she is writing short posts, choosing photographs, and preparing a video about a family that the organisation is supporting. Nadia believes that social media is a powerful tool, but she also knows that it must be used with care. She never shares a photograph without consent, and she always checks her facts before she posts anything. ‘A single mistake can hurt someone,’ she says, ‘and it can damage the trust that we work so hard to build.’ At the end of the day, Nadia feels tired but happy. She knows that her posts have reached thousands of people, and that some of them will help a family in need.

## Part 9  ·  Decision Task
*[OP] Officer track  ·  judgement*


### Part 9: Joseph’s Photograph
*Before you read: can a photo be a problem, even when you have consent for it?*

> Joseph is writing a post about a family that Meridian Relief is helping this winter in Nairobi. The family has agreed to share their story, and they have signed a consent form in their own language. Joseph has a beautiful photograph of the family outside their home, and it would make the post much stronger. The deadline is this evening in Geneva. However, there is a problem. In the background of the photograph, you can clearly see the name of the street and the number of the house. The family gave consent for a photo, but they did not agree to share their exact address. Joseph knows that this information is private, and that sharing it could put the family at risk. Joseph wants the post to be powerful, and he does not want to miss the deadline. But he also knows the most important rule of the organisation: protect people first, and never share private information without permission. He looks at the photograph again and thinks carefully about what to do.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

0. What is Joseph writing about? — A family that the organisation is helping this winter.

1. Did the family give consent for the photograph?
2. What private information can you see in the photograph?
3. Why is this a problem?


### Part 9: Make the Decision
**Should Joseph (a) publish the photograph as it is, (b) hide the address in the photograph and then publish it, or (c) choose a different photograph without the address? Choose one and give reasons.**

**Answer frame:** ‘I think Joseph should ___ , because ___ . Also, ___ . This is better than ___ , because ___ .’

**Model — read this first:**

> Model decision: I think Joseph should hide the address in the photograph and then publish it, because the family gave consent for the photo but not for their address. Their privacy is more important than a stronger post. Sharing an exact address could put the family in danger, and the organisation’s first rule is always to protect people. If Joseph cannot hide the address well, then he should choose a different photograph. In my opinion, it is far better to miss a deadline than to harm a family.

**Phrase bank:** I think… should…  ·  because…  ·  privacy is more important than…  ·  This is better than…  ·  protect people first.

### Part 10: Unit 1 glossary
> communication = sharing information and ideas with people    ·    campaign = a series of actions to reach a goal    ·    consent = permission to use someone’s words or photo    ·    audience = the people who read or watch your work    ·    journalist = a person who reports the news    ·    caption = the short text under a photograph    ·    press release = an official statement sent to the news    ·    feature = a longer article about one topic    ·    platform = a place online where you share content    ·    spokesperson = the person who speaks for an organisation    ·    appeal = a public request for help or money    ·    state verb = a verb about a state or feeling, not an action    ·    routine = something you do regularly    ·    dignity = the respect that every person deserves    ·    communicator = a person whose job is to share information and stories    ·    dignified = shown with respect and self-respect    ·    exaggerate = to make something seem bigger or better than it really is

## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Quantifiers and ‘there has been’
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> There are two cameras in the Geneva office and only one in Nairobi. There are a few recorders, but there is not much storage space, so the team deletes old files every month. There has been a lot of interest in the winter campaign, and there have been many requests for photographs. Notice the difference: we use ‘there is’ and ‘there are’ for the present, and ‘there has been’ and ‘there have been’ when something started in the past and matters now. Notice too that ‘much’ goes with uncountable nouns and ‘many’ goes with countable ones.

**Look at the sentences again. Which nouns are countable? Which are uncountable?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| much / little | with uncountable nouns | amount, not number |  |
| many / few | with countable nouns | number, not amount |  |
| there is / there are | present | There are two cameras here. |  |
| there has / have been | from the past until now | There has been a lot of interest. |  |

**Remember:** Use ‘much’ and ‘little’ with uncountable nouns (money, storage, time) and ‘many’ and ‘few’ with countable nouns (cameras, cards, files). ‘There has been’ connects the past to now.

**Watch out!** Watch out: ‘much’ is unusual in positive sentences. Say ‘a lot of storage’, not ‘much storage’, unless the sentence is negative or a question.

**Gloss:** countable = something you can count one by one    ·    uncountable = something you measure rather than count

### Part 5: The Tools of Visual Storytelling
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> A communications team does not need much equipment, but it needs the right equipment, and it needs to look after it. A camera, a recorder, a tripod and a laptop are enough for most of the work that a small team does. What matters more than the number of tools is the care that the team takes with them. There has been a change in the last ten years. Cameras have become cheaper and lighter, and a good phone can now take a photograph that is strong enough for a report. This is useful for teams that work far from a capital city, where there is not much money and even less time. But a lighter camera has not made the work easier in every way. There are more images than ever, so there is more to check, more to caption and more to store. Storage is the quiet problem of every newsroom: there are only a few people who enjoy sorting files, and there are many who put it off. A good team therefore agrees three simple habits. Copy every file the same day. Write the caption while you still remember the name. Delete nothing until it is in the archive. These habits are not exciting, but they save a story that would otherwise be lost.

> Many communications teams work with very little. There is rarely much money for new equipment, and there are rarely enough people. Yet some of the strongest stories come from the smallest teams. The reason is simple: when there is not much equipment, a team thinks harder about what it is trying to say. A single good photograph, taken with care and with consent, can say more than twenty taken quickly. A short recording of one person speaking clearly can be stronger than a long film with poor sound. There have been many examples of this. A field officer with one phone and a notebook has often brought back a better story than a large crew with three cameras, because the field officer had time to listen. Equipment helps, and nobody should pretend otherwise; a broken microphone has ruined more than one good interview. But the tools that matter most in this work are patience, respect and a clear idea of the story you want to tell, and none of them has to be charged the night before.

### 7B: The Kit-Check Briefing
**🔊 Audio Track 2.5**

*Before you listen: what does a manager need to check before a team goes into the field?*

> Ingrid: Before every field visit, we do a kit-check together, and I want to explain why. There have been three shoots this year where something small went wrong, and each time the cost was not the equipment but the people’s time. First, check the batteries, and check the spares. An empty battery is the most common fault in every office. Second, check the storage. There is never much space on a card, so copy and clear before you travel, not after. Third, check the consent forms, and check that they are in a language the people can actually read. Fourth, check that two people know how to use each piece of equipment, because one person is always ill on the wrong day. And finally, report anything broken the same day. Nobody is in trouble for an honest fault. The only mistake that costs us is the one that nobody mentions until the morning of the shoot.

### Part 8: Reading — The Battery That Almost Stopped the Shoot
*Before you read: what is the smallest thing that could stop a day’s work?*

> Joseph had planned the day carefully. A family in a village outside Nairobi had agreed to tell their story, and they had chosen the morning because the children would be at school. Joseph had the camera, the recorder and the consent forms. He arrived early, greeted the grandmother, explained once more what the photographs would be used for, and sat down to listen. Twenty minutes into the interview, the recorder stopped. The battery was empty. Joseph had charged it the night before, or he thought he had: in fact he had plugged the charger into a socket that did not work. There was no spare in his bag, because the spare was in the office in a different district. He had two choices. He could ask the grandmother to repeat everything, which would waste an hour of her morning and would make her tell the story a second time, less naturally. Or he could write the rest by hand and come back another day for the recording. He chose to write. Then he apologised, explained exactly what had happened, and asked whether he could return on Friday. She laughed and said that she had plenty of time, which was kind but not the point. Since that morning, Joseph has carried two spare batteries. There has not been a repeat.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

0. Where was the family? — In a village outside Nairobi.

1. Why had the family chosen the morning?
2. Why was the battery empty?
3. What did Joseph decide to do?

**Gloss:** spare = an extra one, kept in case the first fails    ·    socket = the place in the wall where you plug something in

### Part 9: One New Piece of Equipment
*Before you read: if you had money for one new thing, what would you buy?*

> The Dhaka office has been given enough money for one new piece of equipment, and Nadia has to choose. There are three good arguments. The first is a second camera. There is only one in the office, and when two field visits happen on the same day, somebody goes without. The second is a set of radio microphones. The sound on the team’s films is often poor, because the single microphone has to sit too far from the speaker, and poor sound loses an audience faster than a poor picture. The third is more storage: a large drive for the archive, because there has been a lot of pressure on space and the team has twice deleted files it later needed. Nadia has asked each of her colleagues, and each of them has named a different one. The money cannot be split, and it must be spent this month. She knows that whatever she chooses, two people will be disappointed, and she wants to be able to explain her reasons clearly to all three.

## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Imperatives, Sequencers and the First Conditional
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Read the consent steps that Layla gives to every new officer in Amman. First, explain what the story is for. Then ask whether the person is happy to take part. Next, read the form aloud, because not everybody reads easily. After that, answer every question honestly. Finally, keep a copy for the person as well as for the file. If the person says no, thank them and leave. If a child is in the photograph, ask the guardian first. Notice two things: the instructions use the imperative, with no subject, and the sequencers — first, then, next, after that, finally — put the steps in order.

**Look at the steps again. Which words are imperatives? Which words put the steps in order?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Imperative | the verb with no subject | instructions and rules |  |
| Negative imperative | do not + verb | things you must never do |  |
| Sequencers | first, then, next, after that, finally | putting steps in order |  |
| First conditional | if + present, will / may | a real possibility and its result |  |

**Remember:** Use the imperative for a rule or an instruction: ‘Ask for consent.’ Use the first conditional for a real possibility: ‘If the person says no, we will stop.’ Never use ‘will’ after ‘if’.

**Watch out!** Watch out: say ‘If the person says no, we will stop’, not ‘If the person will say no’. The ‘will’ goes in the second half only.

**Gloss:** sequencer = a word that shows the order of steps    ·    imperative = the form of a verb used for instructions

## Part 3  ·  Listening and Dialogue

### Part 3: Layla Explains Consent
**🔊 Audio Track 3.2**

*Before you listen: what should a person understand before they agree to be in a story?*

> Layla: Consent is not a signature. It is an understanding, and the signature only records it. So take your time. First, explain what the story is for, where it will appear, and who will see it. Many people imagine a local newsletter and do not realise that a photograph may be seen in another country. Then explain how long we will keep the photograph, and tell them that they can change their mind later. Next, read the form aloud, in the language they read most easily, because not everybody is comfortable reading in front of a stranger. After that, answer every question honestly, even if the honest answer is ‘I do not know’. Finally, give them a copy. If somebody hesitates, that is not a small thing; stop and ask what is worrying them. If you ever feel that a person is agreeing only to be polite, do not take the photograph.

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: Protecting the People in Our Stories
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> Every communications team has a rule that comes before all the others: do no harm. It sounds obvious, and it is not. Harm is rarely dramatic. It is a street sign in the corner of a photograph, a school uniform that shows which school a child attends, or a sentence that says more about a family’s situation than the family realised it was agreeing to. None of these is a lie, and none of them is unkind. Each of them can still put somebody at risk. For this reason the team works through the same steps every time. First, it asks whether the story needs this person at all, or whether the point can be made without them. Then it explains, in the person’s own language, what the story is for and where it will appear. Next, it asks for consent, and it treats hesitation as a no until it is clearly a yes. After that, it checks the words and the images for anything that could identify a home, a school or a route that somebody takes every day. Finally, it tells the person how to withdraw, and it keeps that promise. The team also knows that consent is not the same everywhere. In one country, a signature is a familiar and welcome thing; in another, it is a document that has caused people trouble before. The rule does not change, but the way the team explains it does.

- ○ C) Impossible to prevent

**2. How should a team treat hesitation?**
- ○ A) As a yes
- ○ B) As a no until it is clearly a yes
- ○ C) As a question
- ○ D) As a delay

**3. What does the text say changes between countries?**
- ○ A) The rule itself
- ○ B) The way the rule is explained
- ○ C) The deadline

### Part 5: Consent and Community Across Cultures
**Read about consent in different places. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> Consent is a single principle, but it is not a single conversation. In some communities, a visitor should speak to an elder or a community leader before approaching a family, and to do otherwise would be rude rather than efficient. In others, going through a leader would feel like pressure, and the family would rather decide for themselves. In some places people sign documents every week; in others, a form brought by a stranger is a reason to be careful, and for good reason. A good communications team learns this before it arrives, usually by asking the field staff who live there. What never changes is the substance: the person must understand what will happen, must be free to say no, and must be able to change their mind afterwards. What changes is the route to that understanding — who you speak to first, whether you read the form aloud, how long you leave before you ask again. Teams that confuse the route with the rule make one of two mistakes. They either apply one country’s habits everywhere, or they decide that consent means something different here. Both are wrong, and the second is more dangerous.

0. Consent is a single principle. → T (example)

1. In every community, you should speak to a leader first.   ____
2. A form brought by a stranger can be a reason to be careful.   ____
3. The substance of consent changes from place to place.   ____
4. Deciding that consent means something different here is dangerous.   ____

If somebody hesitates, stop and ask what is worrying them. After that, read the form aloud, answer every question honestly, and give the person a copy with your telephone number. ### Part 6: Why We Protect People (80–120 words)
**Write about why protecting people matters more than a strong story. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> A story that harms somebody is not a strong story; it is a failure. We work with people who have already lost a great deal, and a photograph can take one more thing from them: their safety, or their privacy, or their dignity. For example, a school uniform in the corner of a picture tells a stranger exactly where a child can be found every morning. The family did not agree to that, because nobody thought to mention it. This is why we check every image twice, and why we would rather lose a photograph than a person’s trust.

It also means remembering that a story lasts a long time on the internet, while a conversation lasts five minutes. ### 7B: The Safeguarding Briefing
**🔊 Audio Track 3.5**

*Before you listen: what should a manager say to a team before a visit to a school?*

> Layla: Tomorrow we are visiting a school, so I want to be very clear about four things. First, no child consents alone. The guardian consents, and the child agrees as well — if the child looks uncomfortable, we stop, whatever the form says. Second, no uniforms, no school signs, no gates in any photograph. A uniform tells a stranger where a child is at eight o’clock every morning. Third, no full names for anyone under eighteen, and no classroom details that would narrow it down. Fourth, if you are not sure, the answer is no, and you call me. I would far rather lose twenty photographs than publish one that we cannot take back. And please remember that the children will be excited and will want to be in every picture. That enthusiasm is not consent. It is our job to be the careful ones.

### Part 8: Reading — The Photograph Tomás Did Not Take
*Before you read: have you ever decided not to use something that would have made your work stronger?*

> Tomás was in a health centre in Lima, writing about a new clinic. In the waiting room, a young woman was sitting with her baby, and the light through the window fell on them in a way that photographers wait years for. He asked the nurse whether he could speak to her, and the nurse said that she had come in that morning after a difficult night and was very tired. Tomás went over anyway, introduced himself, and explained what the article was for. The woman said yes immediately. She said yes before he had finished the sentence, and she did not ask a single question. That was what stopped him. He explained again, more slowly: the article would appear on a website that anybody could read, and in a report that went to other countries. She said yes again, and smiled, and looked at the floor. Tomás thanked her, said that he had changed his mind, and left without taking the photograph. Later he wrote in the file: ‘Consent given but not, I think, understood. Tired, unwell, and polite. Do not approach again during treatment.’ The article appeared without a photograph of a patient, and it was a weaker article. He has never regretted it.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

1. Why had the young woman come to the clinic?

3. What did he write in the file?

### Part 9: The Child in the Photograph
*Before you read: what extra care does a story about a child need?*

> The Amman office is publishing a story about a learning centre, and the strongest photograph shows a nine-year-old boy reading aloud to his class. His mother has given written consent, and the boy himself was pleased to be photographed and asked to see the picture afterwards. The learning centre has agreed as well. However, Layla has noticed two things. The boy is wearing the centre’s shirt, which carries its name and the name of the district, and the caption that Tomás has drafted mentions that the boy arrived in the country two years ago. Separately, neither detail is unusual. Together, they tell a reader where this particular child can be found on a weekday morning and something about his family’s situation that his mother may not have meant to publish. The deadline is tomorrow, the photograph is excellent, and nobody has done anything wrong. > Model decision: I think Layla should keep the photograph but blur the shirt and change the caption, because the problem is not the child’s face but the two details that locate him. His mother consented to a photograph, not to a map. Also, the story loses nothing if the caption simply says that the boy enjoys reading aloud. This is better than publishing as it is, because consent was given for something the family did not fully picture, and it is better than dropping the child entirely, because his pleasure in reading is the story.

> consent = permission given freely and with understanding    ·    informed consent = consent given after a full, clear explanation    ·    safeguarding = the work of protecting people, especially children    ·    do no harm = the rule that a story must never put a person at risk    ·    dignity = the respect that every person deserves    ·    anonymous = with the name kept secret    ·    anonymise = to remove the details that identify a person    ·    guardian = the adult responsible for a child    ·    withdraw = to take back a permission you gave before    ·    risk assessment = a check of what could go wrong and for whom    ·    harm = damage or injury to a person    ·    hesitation = a pause because you are not sure    ·    identify = to show who or where somebody is    ·    sequencer = a word that shows the order of steps    ·    imperative = the form of a verb used for instructions

## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Comparatives, Superlatives and ‘as … as’
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Radio is cheaper than a film and faster than a newsletter. SMS is the fastest channel the team has, and it is also the most accessible, because it works on the oldest phone. A newsletter is more detailed than a post, but it reaches far fewer people. Social media is not as reliable as people think: it is the largest channel, but engagement is lower than reach. Notice three forms here: short words add -er and -est, longer words take more and the most, and ‘as … as’ says that two things are equal.

**Look at the sentences again. Which words are comparatives? Which are superlatives?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Comparative | -er / more … than | comparing two things |  |
| Superlative | the -est / the most … | comparing three or more |  |
| as … as | as + adjective + as | two things that are equal |  |
| Irregulars | good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst | common exceptions |  |

**Remember:** Short adjectives add -er and -est (fast → faster → the fastest). Longer adjectives take more and the most (accessible → more accessible → the most accessible). Use ‘as … as’ when two things are the same.

**Watch out!** Watch out: do not say ‘more faster’ or ‘the most fastest’. Use one form only: ‘faster’, ‘the fastest’.

**Gloss:** reliable = something you can trust to work    ·    detailed = containing a lot of information

### Part 3: Nadia Explains the Channels
**🔊 Audio Track 4.2**

*Before you listen: which channel do you use most often, and why?*

> Nadia: Let me explain how we choose a channel, because it is the question I am asked most often. We have five main channels, and none of them is the best one for everything. Social media has the largest reach, but engagement is much lower than reach, and the people it reaches are mostly in cities and mostly younger. The newsletter is far more detailed, and donors read it carefully, but it goes to eleven hundred people, not eleven thousand. Community radio is as important as both of them in the districts where we work, because a radio costs little and needs no data. Bulk SMS is the fastest of all, and it is the most accessible, because it works on the oldest phone. And a press release is the only channel that reaches journalists. So the first question is never ‘which channel is best?’. It is ‘who are we trying to reach, and what do they actually use?’

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: Choosing the Right Channel
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> Communications teams spend a great deal of time arguing about channels, and most of those arguments are really arguments about audiences. A channel is only a way of carrying a message; it has no value on its own. The largest channel is not the best channel, and the newest is rarely the most useful. What matters is a simple pair of questions: who are we trying to reach, and what do those people actually use? The answers are often uncomfortable. A team that is proud of its social media may find that the families it serves are not there at all, and that the account is read mostly by colleagues in other organisations. A team that thinks print is old-fashioned may discover that a single page pinned up in a clinic is read by more people, and more carefully, than a month of posts. Cost matters too, but not in the way people expect. The cheapest channel to produce is often the most expensive to be understood through, because a message that is misread has to be sent again. Accessibility is the measure that teams forget most often: a video with no subtitles excludes anybody who cannot hear it or cannot play it, and a message in one language excludes everybody who does not read that language. The best teams therefore choose two channels rather than one, and they choose them for different audiences, not for the same one twice.

- ○ D) Because it needs translation

**3. What do the best teams do?**

### Part 5: Reaching People Where They Are

> The same message often needs a different channel in each country where an organisation works. In one district, almost everybody has a smartphone and good data, and a short video is the obvious choice. Two hundred kilometres away, data is expensive and the signal is poor, and the same video would simply not be watched. There, a community radio announcement at the right hour reaches more people than any post. In a third place, neither works as well as a notice read aloud at a weekly market. None of these audiences is harder to reach than the others; they are reached differently. The mistake that international teams make most often is to design a message in one place and then send it everywhere, because that is cheaper and faster. It is cheaper only until nobody acts on it. The teams that do this well write the message centrally and choose the channel locally, and they trust the colleague who lives there to say which channel that is.

### Part 6: Compare Two Channels (80–120 words)
**Compare two channels your team uses. Use comparatives, one superlative and one ‘as … as’.**

**Model — read this first:**

> We use two main channels for community messages: radio and SMS. Radio is more trusted locally than anything else we have, and it reaches people who have no phone at all. SMS is faster than radio, and it is the most accessible channel we use, because it works on the oldest handset. However, SMS is not as reliable as radio where the signal is poor. For an announcement that must arrive today, we use both: radio in the morning and SMS in the evening as a reminder. Together they reach more people than either one alone.

**Plan (make notes, then write):** We use…  ___ is more ___ than ___ .  ___ is the most ___ .  ___ is not as ___ as ___ .

**Check before you finish:** ☐ two comparatives?  ☐ one superlative and one ‘as … as’?  ☐ 80–120 words?


### Part 6: How to Reach a Rural District (80–120 words)
**Write about how to reach people in a district with a poor signal. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> Reaching a district with a poor signal is not harder than reaching a city; it is different. The first step is to ask the colleague who lives there, because they know which station people listen to and at what hour. In our experience, community radio in the early evening works better than anything online, and a notice pinned up in the clinic is read more carefully than any post. For example, when the clinic moved last year, the radio announcement reached four hundred households in one evening. The video we had made was watched by eleven people.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear opinion?  ☐ two or three reasons?  ☐ one example?  ☐ 80–120 words?

I would suggest community radio in the morning, because it is more trusted locally than anything we post, and SMS the same evening as a reminder. The signal is poor there, so SMS alone is not as reliable as we would like. Could you check that the announcement is in both languages? Thank you, Nadia.

### Part 6: Reflection — The Right Channel (60–90 words)
**Write about choosing channels. Use your own ideas.**

**Model — read this first:**

> I used to think that the best channel was the one with the most followers. I do not think that now. The best channel is the one that the person I need to reach actually opens, and often that is the smallest and the oldest. A message that nobody reads has no value, however modern it looks. What I have learned is to ask first and design second, and to trust the colleague who lives in the district more than the numbers on my screen.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear main idea?  ☐ reasons or examples?  ☐ 60–90 words?

**🔊 Audio Track 4.5**

*Before you listen: how should a manager explain a channel plan to a team?*

> Ingrid: Before we agree this quarter’s plan, I want to say something about how we choose. We have been getting better at this, but we still make one mistake more often than any other: we design in Geneva and we send everywhere. That is cheaper than doing it properly, and it is cheaper only until nobody acts on the message. So this quarter we are changing the order. The message is written centrally, because it must be the same message. The channel is chosen locally, by the colleague who lives there, and that decision is not mine to overrule. Second, every message goes out on two channels, not one, and they must serve different audiences. Third, accessibility is not an extra. Subtitles, a second language and a format that works on an old phone are part of the job, not a favour. And finally, measure engagement, not only reach. Reach tells you who saw it. Engagement tells you whether it meant anything.

### Part 8: Reading — The Newsletter and the Post
*Before you read: have you ever been surprised by which channel worked best?*

> Last year the Lima office ran the same appeal twice, by accident. Tomás had written a long piece for the monthly newsletter, which goes to eleven hundred donors, and Nadia had made a short post from the same material, which reached forty-one thousand people. On the numbers, there was no contest. The post reached nearly forty times as many people as the newsletter, and the team said so in the monthly report. Then the finance office sent through the figures. The newsletter had raised more than three times as much money as the post, from a hundred and nine people rather than from nine. Nobody had expected this, and the explanation took a while to find. It was not that donors dislike social media. It was that the newsletter arrived in an inbox that the reader had chosen to open, at a moment when they were sitting down, with enough detail to answer the question that a person always asks before they give money: what exactly will this pay for? The post had reached far more people, but it had reached most of them while they were doing something else. The team did not stop posting. But it stopped reporting reach as though reach were the result.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

### Part 9: One Channel for the Clinic
*Before you read: what would you do if the fastest channel was not the one people trust?*

> The Freetown office must tell families in three districts that the mobile clinic is changing its day, from Wednesday to Friday, starting next week. If families arrive on the wrong day, they will have travelled a long way for nothing, and some will not come back. Aisha has three options and enough money for one of them. Bulk SMS is the fastest and the cheapest: it would reach every registered phone within an hour. However, about a third of the families have no phone registered with the clinic, and the signal in the third district is poor. Community radio is more trusted and reaches almost everybody, but the only slot available is on Thursday evening, which is late. Printed notices at the clinic and the two markets would reach the people who come anyway, but not the ones who are most likely to travel on the wrong day. Aisha has until Monday to decide. She would prefer to do all three, and she cannot.

## Part 2  ·  Grammar — The Passive Across Tenses
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Read how a story is made. A draft is written by the officer who did the interview. It is then read by a colleague, and the figures are checked against the project report. While that is happening, the photographs are being edited and matched to their captions. By Thursday, every quote has been read back to the person who said it. The story will be published on Friday, but only after it has been approved by the editor. Notice that the doer is often missing: we say what is done, because who does it is either obvious or not the point.

**Look at the sentences again. Which are present, which are past, and which are future?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Present simple passive | am / is / are + past participle | a routine or a rule |  |
| Past simple passive | was / were + past participle | a finished action |  |
| Present perfect passive | has / have been + past participle | finished, and it matters now |  |
| Future and modal passive | will be / must be + past participle | a plan or an obligation |  |

**Remember:** Use the passive when the doer is obvious, unknown or not important. Add ‘by + the doer’ only when it matters: ‘The draft was written by Tomás.’

**Watch out!** Watch out: do not forget the past participle. Say ‘The story was checked’, not ‘The story was check’.

**Gloss:** past participle = the third form of a verb (write → written, check → checked)    ·    doer = the person or thing that does the action

### Part 3: How a Story Is Written
**🔊 Audio Track 5.2**

*Before you listen: how many people do you think should read a story before it is published?*

> Tomás: Let me explain how a story is made here, because it is not done as it is in a newsroom. First, a draft is written by whoever did the interview, usually within a day, while the conversation is still fresh. Then the draft is sent to a colleague in another office, and that is deliberate: a reader who was not there asks the questions that a reader at home will ask. The figures are checked against the project report, not against memory. Every quote is read back to the person who said it, in their own language, and if they want to change a word, the word is changed. Captions are matched by the photographer, never the writer, because only she knows who is in the picture. Finally, the story is approved by an editor, and nothing is published without that sign-off. It sounds slow. It takes a day longer than writing alone, and it has saved us more than once.

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: How a Story Is Written
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> A humanitarian story is not written in the way a news report is written, and the difference is not style but consequence. A news reporter is accountable to readers; a communications officer is accountable to readers and to the people in the story, who will still be living in that village long after the article has been forgotten. For this reason the writing process is built around checking rather than speed. The draft is written by whoever did the interview, and it is written quickly, while the conversation is fresh. It is then given to a colleague who was not present, because a reader who was not there asks the questions a distant reader will ask: who is this person, what happened first, why does this number matter? Figures are checked against the project report, never against memory, because memory rounds numbers upwards. Quotes are read back to the speaker in the language they used, and if the speaker wants a word changed, the word is changed; a quote is a record of what somebody chose to say, not a trophy. Captions are written by the photographer, who alone knows who is in the frame. Finally, an editor signs the piece off, and nothing goes out without that signature. Teams that skip a step usually skip the read-back, because it is the slowest and the least visible. It is also the one that protects the person who trusted you.

0. The writing process is built around checking. (example)

**1. Who is a communications officer accountable to?**
- ○ A) Readers only
- ○ B) Readers and the people in the story
- ○ C) Donors only
- ○ D) Editors only

**2. Why is the draft given to a colleague who was not present?**
- ○ A) Because they write faster
- ○ B) Because they ask the questions a distant reader will ask
- ○ C) Because they know the village

### Part 5: Telling the Truth, Protecting the Person
**Read about truth and protection in writing. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> Two duties sit beside each other in every humanitarian story, and sometimes they pull in different directions. The first is to tell the truth: not to exaggerate, not to invent, not to let a strong sentence carry a weak fact. The second is to protect the people in the story, who are rarely in a position to protect themselves once a text has been published. Most of the time these duties agree. A true story, carefully told, is also a safe one. But occasionally they do not. A detail may be true and important and still dangerous: the name of a street, a scar, a job, the fact that a family was the only one in the village to receive something. When that happens, the rule is not to choose between truth and protection. It is to find the version that is both. Usually it exists. The street can become ‘a district in the north’. The scar can simply not be mentioned. What is never acceptable is to publish a false detail in order to protect somebody, because a reader who later discovers it will stop believing the parts that were true.

1. The two duties always agree.   ____
2. A detail can be true and still dangerous.   ____
3. It is acceptable to publish a false detail to protect somebody.   ____

### Part 6: Describe How a Story Is Written (80–120 words)
**Describe how a story is written and checked in your organisation. Use at least four passive sentences.**

**Model — read this first:**

> In our team, a story is never published by one person alone. A draft is written by the officer who did the interview, usually on the same day. It is then sent to a colleague in another office, who reads it as a stranger would. The figures are checked against the project report, and every quote is read back to the person who said it, in their own language. The captions are written by the photographer, because only she knows who is in the picture. Finally, the piece is approved by an editor. Nothing is published without that sign-off.

### Part 6: Why Every Story Is Checked (80–120 words)
**Write about why every story must be checked. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> Checking is not a sign that we do not trust each other; it is a sign that we take the work seriously. A figure that is wrong by twenty families is still wrong when it is quoted back to us a year later. A quote that was never read back may not be what the speaker meant, and they cannot correct it once it is published. For example, last year a figure was taken from the wrong monthly report, and it was found only because a colleague asked where the number came from. One question saved the whole article.

### 7B: The Writing-Standards Briefing
**🔊 Audio Track 5.5**

*Before you listen: what standards would you set for a team’s writing?*

> Ingrid: I want to go through our writing standards, because two of them were missed last month and I would rather explain than correct. First, every figure is checked against the written report, not against what somebody remembers. Memory rounds numbers upwards, always in our favour, and that is how an organisation loses its reputation. Second, every quote is read back to the speaker in the language they used. If they want a word changed, the word is changed, and we record that it was done. A quote belongs to the person who said it. Third, captions are written by the photographer. Only she knows who is in the frame, and a wrong name under a face is one of the few mistakes we cannot really repair. Fourth, the sign-off happens in the morning, not at six in the evening, so that there is time to fix whatever it finds. And finally, if a detail cannot be confirmed, it is removed. It is not softened, and it is not qualified. Removed.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

### Part 8: Reading — The Story That Was Rewritten
*Before you read: have you ever had to rewrite something you were proud of?*

> The piece had been written in a morning, and Tomás was pleased with it. A mother in a village outside Lima had described, in her own words, the night the river rose and what she had carried out of the house. The detail was extraordinary: the two things she chose, the neighbour who helped, the shoes she lost on the path. It was the strongest thing he had written that year. Nadia read it as the outside reader and sent back one line: ‘Has this been read back to her?’ It had not. Joseph called the following morning and read the article aloud, sentence by sentence, in the language of the interview. The mother listened to the whole thing without speaking. Then she said that it was all true, and asked for two changes. She did not want the shoes mentioned, because her children would read it and would feel ashamed. And she did not want the neighbour named, because the neighbour had not been asked. Both details were true, and both were removed. The article that was published was quieter than the one that had been written, and Tomás thought at first that it was weaker. Reading it again a month later, he decided it was not weaker. It was hers.

### Part 9: A Detail That Could Identify
*Before you read: can one small detail make a whole story unsafe?*

> The Lima office has a strong piece about a woman who has started a small business after a flood. She has given full consent, the quotes have been read back, and she is happy for her first name and her photograph to be used. The problem is one sentence near the end. It says that she is the only woman in her district running a workshop of this kind. Tomás included it because it is true and because it explains why her story matters. Nadia, reading as the outside reader, has pointed out that the sentence identifies her completely: anyone who knows the district knows exactly who this is, whatever name is used. The woman herself is not worried, and says so. But she has not been asked about the one sentence specifically, only about the article in general, and there has been trouble in that district before about who receives support and who does not. The piece is due to be published on Friday, and the sentence is the best line in it.

Also, she knows the district far better than we do, and whether the sentence is safe is her judgement and not ours. ## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Modals: Requests, Advice and Deduction
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Read what Tomás says to a new colleague. ‘Could you come with me this morning? You should listen more than you speak, and you shouldn’t write while somebody is talking. If the answer is short, you might ask a follow-up, but you must not suggest the answer yourself. She has not replied to my message, so she must be busy, or she might be travelling. She can’t have forgotten; she wrote to me yesterday.’ Notice three uses of modals here: could for a request, should for advice, and must, might and can’t for how sure we are.

**Look at the sentences again. Which modals make a request? Which give advice? Which show how sure the speaker is?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests | could / would you… | asking politely |  |
| Advice | should / shouldn’t | saying what is a good idea |  |
| Deduction: sure | must / can’t | almost certain, from evidence |  |
| Deduction: possible | might / may / could | possible, but not certain |  |

**Remember:** Use ‘must’ when you are almost sure something is true, and ‘can’t’ when you are almost sure it is not. Use ‘might’, ‘may’ or ‘could’ when it is only possible.

**Watch out!** Watch out: for deduction, the opposite of ‘must be’ is ‘can’t be’, not ‘mustn’t be’. ‘Mustn’t’ means that something is forbidden.

**Gloss:** deduction = a conclusion you reach from the evidence you have    ·    evidence = the facts that help you decide what is true

## Part 3  ·  Listening and Dialogue

### Part 3: Tomás Explains Interviewing
**🔊 Audio Track 6.2**

*Before you listen: what makes a good interviewer, in your opinion?*

> Tomás: People think interviewing is about asking good questions. It is mostly about listening, and about being comfortable with silence. My first question is always open and easy: could you tell me about your day? It lets the person choose where to begin, and where somebody begins tells you a great deal. After that, almost everything should be a follow-up. If an answer is short, do not move to the next question on your list; ask about the answer you just received. You should never ask a leading question — ‘That must have been frightening, wasn’t it?’ — because the person will agree with you out of politeness and you will publish your own words in their mouth. With an interpreter, look at the person, not the interpreter, and allow twice as much time. And remember that the interview can stop at any moment. If somebody looks tired or upset, put the recorder down. The story is never worth more than the person telling it.

*While you listen: write True (T) or False (F). (0. is done.)*

3. A leading question can put your words in the person’s mouth.   ____
4. With an interpreter, you should look at the interpreter.   ____

**Useful phrases:** Could you tell me about your day?  ·  Ask about the answer you just received.  ·  Put the recorder down.


### Part 3: Tomás Interviews Mrs Dela Cruz
**🔊 Audio Track 6.3**

*Before you listen: how would you begin an interview with somebody you have never met?*

> Tomás: Thank you for your time. Could you tell me about your day?  
> Mrs Dela Cruz: It starts early. I am at the market by five, and I am home by two.  
> Tomás: By five. What is the market like at that hour?  
> Mrs Dela Cruz: Quiet. The good fish goes first, so you must be early or you buy nothing.  
> Tomás: And you have been doing this for how long?  
> Mrs Dela Cruz: Eleven years. Since the first flood.  
> Tomás: You said ‘the first’. Would you tell me about that?  
> Mrs Dela Cruz: Maybe another day. Not this morning.  
> Tomás: Of course. Thank you for saying so. Could I ask instead what you would like people to know about the market?  
> Mrs Dela Cruz: That it is not a sad place. People laugh there.

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: The Art of the Interview
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> Most new communications officers prepare for an interview by writing a list of questions, and most of them discover, somewhere around the third interview, that the list is the problem. A list makes you listen for the moment when you can ask the next thing on it, rather than listening to what is actually being said. The officers who are good at this prepare differently. They write down two or three things they genuinely want to understand, and then they put the paper away. The first question should be open and easy, because its job is not to collect information but to let the person choose where to begin. Where somebody begins is itself information. After that, almost every question should be a follow-up: ‘you said the first flood — would you tell me about that?’ Follow-ups show that you were listening, which is the only thing that makes a stranger willing to continue. There are two rules that should never be broken. Never ask a leading question, because a polite person will agree with you and you will end up publishing your own opinion in somebody else’s words. And never continue when somebody is tired, upset or simply finished. An interview that is stopped early can be continued another day. An interview that is pushed too far usually cannot be repaired, and the person is left feeling that they were a source rather than a human being.

0. Many new officers prepare by writing a list of questions. (example)

- ○ A) It is too short
- ○ B) It makes you listen for your next question
- ○ C) It is hard to carry
- ○ D) It is written down

**2. What is the job of the first question?**
- ○ A) To collect facts
- ○ B) To let the person choose where to begin
- ○ C) To fill time
- ○ D) To test the recorder

**3. Why should you never ask a leading question?**
- ○ A) It takes too long
- ○ B) A polite person will agree with you
- ○ C) It is hard to translate

### Part 5: Listening Across Languages
**Read about interviewing through an interpreter. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> A great many interviews in international work are done through an interpreter, and they are not simply slower versions of ordinary interviews. They are a different skill. The first thing to accept is the time: everything takes at least twice as long, and an interview planned for thirty minutes should be given an hour. The second is where you look. It is natural to look at the person who is speaking your language, but if you look at the interpreter, the person being interviewed will quickly feel that they are talking to a machine. Look at them, even while you cannot understand a word. The third is the brief you give the interpreter beforehand: ask for a full translation rather than a summary, and ask them to translate hesitations and unfinished sentences too, because those carry meaning. The fourth is the quote. A quote that has travelled through two languages is not the person’s exact words, and it should not be presented as though it were. Honest teams write ‘speaking through an interpreter’ and read the final version back in the original language before they publish it.

0. Interviews through an interpreter take longer. → T (example)

### Part 6: How to Interview with Respect (80–120 words)
**Write advice for a new interviewer. Use should, shouldn’t and one deduction modal.**

**Model — read this first:**

> You should begin with an open, easy question, because it lets the person choose where to begin. You shouldn’t work from a list, since a list makes you listen for your next question instead of for the answer. Almost every question after the first should be a follow-up. You should never ask a leading question: a polite person will agree with you, and you will publish your own words in their mouth. If somebody looks tired, they probably are, and you should stop. An interview that is stopped early can be continued another day.

### Part 6: Open Questions or Closed Questions? (80–120 words)
**Write about when to use open and closed questions. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> Open questions and closed questions do different jobs, and a good interview uses both. Open questions invite a person to speak in their own way, and they belong at the beginning and whenever you want to understand rather than confirm. Closed questions belong at the end, when you need one clear fact: a date, a number, a spelling. The mistake is to use a closed question when you want a story. For example, ‘Were you frightened?’ can only be answered yes or no, and it also suggests the answer. ‘How did you feel?’ gives the person the whole room.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear opinion?  ☐ two or three reasons?  ☐ one example?  ☐ 80–120 words?

### 7B: The Interview-Coaching Briefing
**🔊 Audio Track 6.5**

*Before you listen: how should a manager give feedback after a difficult interview?*

> Ingrid: Before we go out tomorrow, I want to say something about how we coach each other on interviews, because it is the part of the work people find hardest to hear feedback on. Start by asking the officer how they thought it went. Almost always they will name the problem themselves, and feedback that somebody has named themselves is feedback they can use. Then name one thing that genuinely worked, and be specific: ‘your first question was open and easy’ is useful, ‘that was good’ is not. After that, offer one thing to change — one, not four — and make it concrete enough to practise. ‘Listen better’ is useless advice. ‘Count to five before you speak again’ is advice somebody can follow tomorrow. And finally, offer to go together next time. Interviewing is a craft, and nobody has ever improved at it by being told that they should have done better.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

### Part 8: Reading — The Answer Tomás Almost Missed
*Before you read: has anybody ever told you something important just as you were leaving?*

> The interview had been short and, Tomás thought, disappointing. He had met a man in Nairobi who ran a repair workshop that Meridian Relief had helped to restart after a fire, and the answers had been polite and brief. Yes, the workshop was busy. Yes, the support had helped. No, there was nothing else he wanted to say. Tomás thanked him, switched off the recorder, and began packing his bag. The man watched him for a moment and then said, quietly, that the hardest part had not been the fire. The hardest part had been the four months afterwards, when he had had nothing to do, and his children had watched him sit in the house. Tomás stopped. He asked whether he could switch the recorder on again, and explained that this was the part of the story that people would understand. The man thought about it and said yes, but only if the children were not mentioned. The interview that followed lasted forty minutes and was the best Tomás recorded that year. Afterwards he wrote one line in his notes, which he has kept since: ‘The recorder goes off last, not first. People often decide to tell you something at the moment they think the interview has ended.’

### Part 9: Off the Record
*Before you read: what does it mean when somebody says ‘this is off the record’?*

> During an interview in Nairobi about a water project, a community leader told Joseph something important and then added, after he had said it, that it was off the record. He had described a delay: the pipes had arrived three months late, and the reason, he said, was a dispute between two local offices that had nothing to do with the community. The delay is public knowledge and is mentioned in the project report. The reason is not. Joseph is now writing the article, and the delay needs explaining, because readers in other countries will ask why a simple project took a year. Without the reason, the article implies that the community was slow, which is untrue and unfair to them. With the reason, Joseph would be publishing something a person asked him not to publish, even though he asked afterwards rather than before. Joseph could go back and ask the leader whether the reason can be used, with or without his name. That would take two days, and the article is due on Friday.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

0. What was late? — The pipes, by three months.

1. What is public knowledge, and what is not?
2. What does the article imply if the reason is left out?
3. What could Joseph do, and how long would it take?


### Part 9: Make the Decision
**Should Joseph (a) publish the reason, since the delay is public, (b) leave the reason out, or (c) delay the article and ask the leader? Choose one and give reasons.**

**Answer frame:** ‘I think Joseph should ___ , because ___ . Also, ___ . This is better than ___ , because ___ .’

**Model — read this first:**

> Model decision: I think Joseph should delay the article and ask the leader, because ‘off the record’ was said late but it was still said, and breaking it would cost us a relationship that took years to build. Also, the leader may well agree to the reason being used without his name, which would solve the problem completely. This is better than leaving the reason out, because an article that implies the community was slow is unfair to the very people we are writing about, and two days is a small price for getting it right.

**Phrase bank:** I think… should…  ·  because…  ·  it would cost us a relationship  ·  This is better than…  ·  ask, rather than guess what somebody meant.

### Part 2: Notice
> Read what Ingrid says at the planning meeting. ‘We are going to launch the winter campaign on the first of March; that decision is made. We are meeting the donors on Tuesday — it is in the diary. The radio slot starts at six in the evening, because that is when the programme always begins. I will send you the one-page plan this afternoon; I have just decided that. And if the funding does not arrive by the twentieth, we will move the launch by a week.’ Notice four ways of talking about the future, and one conditional.

**Look at the sentences again. Which decisions were made before today? Which was made at that moment?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| going to | a decision already taken | We are going to launch in March. |  |
| present continuous | a fixed arrangement, usually with a time | We are meeting the donors on Tuesday. |  |
| will | a decision made now, or a prediction | I will send it this afternoon. |  |
| present simple | a timetable | The programme starts at six. |  |

**Remember:** Use ‘going to’ for a plan you already have, the present continuous for an arrangement in the diary, and ‘will’ for a decision you make as you speak. After ‘if’, use the present.

**Watch out!** Watch out: say ‘If the funding arrives, we will begin’, not ‘If the funding will arrive’. The ‘will’ belongs in the second half.

**Gloss:** arrangement = something you have agreed with another person    ·    prediction = what you think will happen

## Part 3  ·  Listening and Dialogue
*[OP] Officer track  ·  listening*


### Part 3: Ingrid Explains Planning
**🔊 Audio Track 7.2**

*Before you listen: what should be written on a campaign plan?*

> Ingrid: A campaign plan should fit on one page, and if it does not, the campaign is probably too complicated. At the top, write the objective as a single sentence that anybody in the organisation could read and understand. Not ‘raise awareness’ — that means nothing. Something you could count: four thousand families will know that the clinic has moved. Underneath, list the audiences, and beside each one, the channel that actually reaches it. Then the timeline: every step, its date and the name of the person who owns it. A task with no owner does not happen; a task with three owners happens twice or not at all. At the bottom, Plan B. What will we do if the funding is late, if the interpreter is ill, if it rains on the launch day? Write it down before you need it, because nobody thinks clearly in the week of a launch. And then put the page on the wall, where everybody can see it.

*While you listen: write True (T) or False (F). (0. is done.)*

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: How to Plan a Campaign
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> Most campaign plans fail in the same two places, and neither of them is the idea. The first is the objective. A great many plans begin with something like ‘raise awareness’, which cannot be measured, cannot be disproved and therefore cannot be managed. A usable objective says who will know or do what, and by when: four thousand families in three districts will know that the clinic has moved, before the first of March. That sentence can be checked afterwards, which is uncomfortable and is exactly the point. The second place plans fail is ownership. Every step on a timeline needs one name beside it. A task owned by ‘the team’ is owned by nobody; a task owned by three people is usually done twice or not at all, and the person who notices the gap is always the one with the least time to fix it. Beyond those two, the discipline is honesty. Put in the dates you will actually meet, not the ones that look impressive. Build a margin into the steps that depend on somebody outside the team, because those are the ones that slip. And write Plan B before you need it, when you are calm, rather than in the week of the launch, when nobody thinks clearly and the loudest voice usually wins. A plan is not a promise that nothing will change. It is an agreement about what everybody will do when it does.

0. Most campaign plans fail in two places. (example)

**1. What is wrong with ‘raise awareness’ as an objective?**
- ○ A) It is too long
- ○ B) It cannot be measured
- ○ C) It is too expensive
- ○ D) It is not ambitious

**2. What happens to a task owned by three people?**
- ○ A) It is done well
- ○ B) It is done twice or not at all
- ○ C) It is cancelled
- ○ D) It is done early

**3. When should Plan B be written?**
- ○ A) In the week of the launch
- ○ B) Before you need it
- ○ C) After the campaign
- ○ D) Never

### Part 5: Planning for Real Life in the Field
**Read about planning in difficult conditions. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> A plan made in a head office and a plan made in a field office are different documents, even when they share a page. In a capital city, a delay of two days is an inconvenience. In a district where the road is passable for part of the year, where the electricity comes on in the evening, and where the interpreter is also the only nurse, two days can move a launch by a month. Teams that plan well across both places do three things. They ask the field office for the dates rather than proposing them, because only the field office knows which week the market is held and which week nobody will be at home. They build margin into every step that depends on somebody outside the team, and they put that margin in the plan where everybody can see it, rather than hiding it in their own heads. And they agree in advance what will happen if a step slips: not ‘we will discuss it’, which means an argument in the worst week, but a decision taken calmly in advance. None of this makes a plan more likely to survive unchanged. It makes the team more likely to survive the change.

0. A delay of two days can matter more in a district. → T (example)

**Write about why a team should prepare a Plan B. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> A Plan B is not pessimism; it is the only way to stay calm in the week of a launch. If the decision has already been taken, calmly, in advance, then nobody has to argue about it at nine o’clock at night. For example, last year our funding confirmation arrived four days late. *Before you listen: how should a manager run a planning meeting?*

> Ingrid: Three things before we start planning, because we have made the same mistakes twice now. First, we are not leaving this room with an objective that cannot be counted. ‘Raise awareness’ is not an objective; it is a wish. I want a sentence with a number, a place and a date in it, and I want it written at the top of the page. Second, every single step gets one name. Not a team, not two names, one.
