### Part 8: Reading — The Plan That Changed
*Before you read: what is the latest a plan has ever changed on you?*

> The plan had been on the wall for five weeks, and it was a good one. The winter appeal would launch on the first of March at eight in the morning: the article live, the first post at eight, the radio announcement the same evening in both languages, and a second post at midday with Aisha’s photographs. Every step had one name beside it. On the twenty-seventh of February, the road to the eastern district closed. It was not dramatic — heavy rain, a bridge that the district had been worrying about for two years — but it meant that Joseph could not reach the radio station, and that the photographs of the distribution point, which were the heart of the appeal, did not exist yet. Five weeks of planning had not prevented this and could not have done. What the plan did was narrower and more useful. Because Plan B had been written in January, when everybody was calm, nobody spent the twenty-eighth arguing. The radio announcement was recorded in Nairobi instead and sent to the station as a file. The appeal launched with photographs from the clinic rather than the distribution point, and Aisha’s pictures were added on the fourth. The objective was met eleven days later than planned. Nobody shouted at anybody.

### Part 9: When to Launch
*Before you read: is it better to launch late, or to launch with less?*

> The Dhaka office is four days from the launch of a campaign about a new water point, and two things have gone wrong at once. The photographs have not arrived, because Aisha could not reach the site, and the funding confirmation that the appeal was going to quote has been delayed by the donor until the middle of the month. Nadia has three options. She can launch on time with the photographs from last year’s campaign, which are good but are not of this water point, and without the figure. She can delay the whole campaign by two weeks, which is clean but means launching after the rains begin, when the families who most need the message will be hardest to reach. Or she can launch on time with the article and the radio announcement only, and add the photographs and the figure as a second wave on the fourteenth. Each option costs something. The team has agreed in advance that the objective — four thousand families knowing about the water point — matters more than the appearance of the launch, and Nadia is the owner of this decision.

### Part 2: Notice
> Read the standards that Layla reads out to every new officer. ‘You must check every figure against the written report. You mustn’t publish a name that has not been consented to. |  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| must / have to | it is necessary | You must check every figure. |  |
| mustn’t | it is forbidden | You mustn’t publish an unconsented name. |  |
| don’t have to | it is not necessary | You don’t have to send every post. |  |
| may / can | it is permitted | You may keep the form for three years. |  |

**Remember:** ‘Mustn’t’ and ‘don’t have to’ are opposites, not the same. When you report a rule, ‘must’ usually becomes ‘had to’: She said that we had to check every figure.

**Watch out!** Watch out: say ‘You mustn’t share the form’ when it is forbidden, and ‘You don’t have to share the form’ when it is simply not necessary. The two sentences mean opposite things.

**Gloss:** obligation = something you are required to do    ·    permission = being allowed to do something

### Part 3: Layla Explains the Rules
**🔊 Audio Track 8.2**

*Before you listen: which rule in your work is the hardest to follow?*

> Layla: Our standards are the same in all six offices, and each office must also follow the law of its own country. Where the two differ, you follow the stricter one. That answers most questions. Now the specific ones. You must check every figure against the written report. You mustn’t publish a name, face or location not consented to for that use. You don’t have to send every post to the editor — that would be unworkable — but anything that names a person, a place or a figure has to be signed off. On data: we keep only what we need — data minimisation — and only for as long as the policy says. A consent form may be kept for three years; after that it must be deleted, and deleted means deleted, not moved to somebody’s desktop. And if we publish something wrong, we correct it openly and say what was wrong. We do not quietly edit a post and hope nobody noticed.

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading

### Part 5: Rules That Protect People
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> Communications standards are often described as a burden, and in a busy week they feel like one. It is worth remembering what each of them is actually for. The rule that every figure must be checked against a written report exists because memory rounds numbers in the organisation’s favour, never against it, and because a figure that is wrong by a little is quoted back for years. The rule that a name, a face or a location must not be published without consent for that particular use exists because consent is specific: a person who agreed to a photograph in a local newsletter did not agree to a donor report read in six countries. The rule that personal data is kept only as long as it is needed exists because data nobody uses is data somebody can lose. And the rule that a published mistake is corrected openly, on the same channel, in the same week, exists because the alternative — quietly editing a post and hoping — destroys more trust in one evening than a correction ever has. An organisation working in six countries must also accept that its own standards are not the whole picture. Each office follows the law where it works, and where the two differ, the stricter rule applies. That is inconvenient, and it is not negotiable, because the person protected by the stricter rule does not care which document it came from.

**3. What happens where the standards and the law differ?**

### Part 5: Privacy and Trust Across Borders
**Read about data across countries. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> An organisation that works in several countries holds personal data that crosses borders every day, usually without anybody thinking about it. A consent form signed in one country is scanned and stored on a server in another. A list of beneficiaries is attached to an email and read in a third. None of this is unusual, and none of it is automatically wrong, but it means that the question ‘who can see this, and under which country’s law?’ has to be asked before the file is created rather than after it has been shared. The practical answer most teams reach is data minimisation: collect less, keep it for less time, and share only what the other person actually needs. A donor who wants to know whether a project works does not need names; they need numbers. A colleague in another office who is editing an article does not need the consent forms; they need to know that consent exists. Teams that apply this habit find that most difficult questions never arise, because the data that would have caused the problem was never collected in the first place.

*Before you listen: what should a manager say when a rule is inconvenient?*

> Layla: I want to talk about the moment when a rule is inconvenient, because that is the only moment a rule matters. Everybody follows the standards on a quiet Tuesday. The test is Thursday evening, when a donor is waiting and the figure has not been confirmed. So, three things. First, when the rule and the deadline disagree, the rule wins, and I would rather publish a day late than publish a name that nobody consented to. Second, if somebody outside this organisation is pushing you — a donor, a journalist, a government office — that is my job, not yours. Say that you have to check and send them to me. You are not required to argue with anybody senior. Third, if we get it wrong, we correct it openly, on the same channel, in the same week, and we say what was wrong. Nobody has ever been in trouble here for a correction. People have been in trouble for a quiet edit.

### Part 8: Reading — The Detail in the Corner
*Before you read: have you ever found a problem in something that had already been published?*

> The article had been live for six days before anybody noticed. It was a good piece about a school feeding programme in Amman, carefully checked: every figure against the report, every name consented, every quote read back. The photograph showed a classroom from the back, which is how the team almost always photographs children — no faces, no uniforms, no signs. What nobody had noticed was a sheet of paper pinned to the wall in the corner of the frame, slightly out of focus but readable if you enlarged it. It was a class list, with eleven first names and surnames. A colleague in another organisation spotted it and emailed, privately and kindly, on a Sunday. Layla took the article down within the hour, which was the easy part. The harder question was what to say. Some of the team wanted to replace the photograph quietly and say nothing, on the grounds that mentioning it would draw attention to a list that almost nobody had seen. Layla disagreed. The article was republished the next morning with a different photograph and a correction notice explaining that an earlier image had been removed because it contained personal information. Two readers wrote to thank her. Nobody wrote to complain. The team now enlarges every photograph before publication, and the habit has caught three more things in a year.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

1. What was in the corner of the photograph?
2. What did some of the team want to do?
3. What does the team now do before publication?

### Part 9: The Deadline and the Data
*Before you read: what would you do if a donor asked for something you are not allowed to give?*

> A donor who funds the Geneva office’s largest programme has asked for the full beneficiary list before Friday: names, villages and household sizes, for four hundred families. The request has come from a new officer at the donor, who says that their audit department requires it and that the next payment cannot be approved without it. The payment is due on Monday, and three country offices are expecting it. Ingrid knows the rule: identifying personal data is not shared outside the organisation without consent for that purpose, and nobody consented to a donor audit. She also knows that the people in the list cannot be asked in two days, and that an anonymised summary — household sizes by village, no names — would answer every reasonable audit question. But the donor’s officer has said, politely, that a summary is not what their process asks for. Ingrid has until Thursday evening. She can also ask the donor’s own data-protection officer, whom she has never met, but that will take longer than two days.

> Model decision: I think Ingrid should send an anonymised summary and explain clearly why, because the families never consented to a donor audit and we cannot ask four hundred of them in two days. Also, a summary answers every reasonable audit question, and most donors accept it once somebody explains the rule rather than simply refusing. This is better than sending the list, because a payment we obtained by breaking our own promise is not worth having, and it is faster than writing to a data-protection officer we have never met.

### Part 10: Unit 8 glossary
> policy = the official rules an organisation follows    ·    standard = the level of quality that is expected    ·    personal data = information that identifies a living person    ·    data minimisation = collecting and keeping only what you really need    ·    retention period = how long information may be kept    ·    correction notice = a public statement of what was wrong    ·    right of reply = the chance to answer a criticism before publication    ·    embargo = a date before which information must not be published    ·    sign-off = the final approval before publication    ·    privacy = the right to keep your information to yourself    ·    obligation = something you are required to do    ·    permission = being allowed to do something    ·    anonymised = with the names and identifying details removed    ·    audit = an official check of records    ·    negotiable = open to discussion and change

## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Present Perfect Continuous and Past Continuous
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Read Ingrid’s note from the morning of the crisis. ‘The crisis desk has been running since six. We have been answering calls all morning, and we have published three updates so far. The rumour started on Tuesday evening, and it was spreading quickly before anybody told us. I was checking the figure when the first journalist called, which is why the answer took so long.’ Notice the difference: ‘has been running’ and ‘have been answering’ are activities that are still going on; ‘started’ is finished; and ‘was checking’ and ‘was spreading’ are the background to something else.

**Look at the sentences again. Which activities are still going on? Which are the background to another event?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Present perfect continuous | have / has been + -ing | an activity continuing up to now |  |
| Present perfect simple | have / has + past participle | how many, or a finished result |  |
| Past continuous | was / were + -ing | the background to a past event |  |
| Past simple | the -ed or irregular form | the event itself |  |

**Remember:** Use the present perfect continuous for how long an activity has gone on, and the present perfect simple for how many things are finished. Use the past continuous for what was already happening when something else occurred.

**Watch out!** Watch out: state verbs do not usually take the continuous. Say ‘We have known since six’, not ‘We have been knowing since six’.

**Gloss:** background = what was already happening when something else occurred    ·    occur = to happen

## Part 3  ·  Listening and Dialogue

### Part 3: Ingrid Explains Crisis Work
**🔊 Audio Track 9.2**

*Before you listen: what would you say publicly in the first hour of a crisis?*

> Ingrid: In a crisis, people remember not what you said but whether you were steady. So we have four habits. First, publish something within the hour: what has happened, what we are doing, and when the next update will come. It will be short, and that is fine. Second, never guess. If a fact has not been verified, say that it has not been verified. ‘We do not yet know’ is a complete and honest answer, and it is far better than a number you have to withdraw tomorrow. Third, update at the time you promised, even if nothing has changed, because silence is where rumours grow; if you have nothing new, say that you have nothing new. Fourth, one voice. One named person speaks for us, and everybody else sends questions to that person — not because colleagues are untrustworthy, but because five slightly different answers become the story. And afterwards we write down what we have learned, while we still remember it.

*While you listen: write True (T) or False (F). (0. is done.)*

1. A short first statement is acceptable.   ____

3. The team updates only when there is news.   ____
4. Several people may speak for the organisation.   ____

**Useful phrases:** We do not yet know.  ·  Silence is where rumours grow.  ·  One named person speaks for us.


### Part 3: Handling a Rumour
**🔊 Audio Track 9.3**

*Before you listen: how would you answer a rumour that is not true?*

> Nadia: Ingrid, there is a message going round that we have stopped the food distribution in the north.  
> Ingrid: Where did it start?  
> Nadia: A community group shared it on Tuesday evening. It has been spreading all morning.  
> Ingrid: Have we verified what is actually happening there?  
> Nadia: Joseph has been calling the district since eight. Two of the three sites are open. The third closed for one day because the road was flooded.  
> Ingrid: Then we say exactly that. Do not repeat the rumour in the headline — people remember the first thing they read. Lead with what is true: two sites open, one closed for a day, reopening tomorrow.  
> Nadia: And if they ask why nobody told them?  
> Ingrid: Then we say that we should have told them on Tuesday, and that we are sorry. That is also true.

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: Communicating in a Crisis
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> Crisis communication is often called a skill in writing; it is mostly a skill in deciding. The writing itself is simple: short sentences, no decoration, nothing you cannot prove. The difficulty is that every decision has to be made while the facts are still arriving and while somebody more senior is asking why there has not been a statement yet. Four habits make this bearable. The first is to publish quickly and shortly. A statement within the hour that says what has happened, what the organisation is doing and when the next update will come is worth more than a careful one three hours later, because in those three hours other people have been explaining your situation for you. The second is never to guess. ‘We do not yet know’ is a complete answer, and it is the only one that is still true tomorrow. A number that has to be withdrawn costs more trust than a silence ever did. The third is to update at the promised time whether or not there is news, because silence is read as concealment, and a team that has been steady for six hours is believed at the seventh. The fourth is the single voice: one named person answers, since five slightly different answers become the story instead of the event. Afterwards, write down what you have learned while you still remember it, because nobody remembers a crisis accurately a month later.

0. Crisis communication is mostly a skill in deciding. (example)

**1. Why publish quickly and shortly?**
- ○ A) To look efficient
- ○ B) Because others will explain your situation for you
- ○ C) Because it is cheaper
- ○ D) Because donors require it

**2. What does the text say about ‘we do not yet know’?**
- ○ A) It is weak
- ○ B) It is a complete answer
- ○ C) It should be avoided
- ○ D) It is only for journalists

**3. Why is silence a problem?**
- ○ A) It is read as concealment
- ○ B) It is impolite
- ○ C) It is expensive
- ○ D) It is slow

### Part 5: A Steady Voice Across Time Zones
**Read about crisis work in an international team. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> A crisis in an organisation that works across six time zones has a particular problem: it begins while most of the team is asleep. The office nearest the event is the one that knows most and usually the one with the fewest communications staff, and by the time Geneva wakes up, six hours of conversation have already happened without it. Teams that handle this well decide three things in advance. They agree who may publish a holding statement without waiting for anybody else, and they make that authority local rather than central, because a statement four hours late is worse than a statement that a manager would have worded differently. They agree a handover: the desk moves with the working day, and the team that is going to sleep writes down what it knows, what it has verified and who it has promised to call. And they agree one voice per language rather than one voice in total, because a journalist in Dhaka will not wait for Geneva and should not have to. None of this removes the difficulty. It stops the team from spending the first three hours deciding who is allowed to speak.

Never guess — if a fact has not been verified, say so, because ‘we do not yet know’ is still true tomorrow and a withdrawn number is not. ### Part 6: Why We Correct Rumours (80–120 words)
**Write about why an organisation should answer rumours. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> A rumour that is not answered becomes the record. People do not usually read a correction a week later; they remember the first version they saw, and after a few days it is simply what they know. Answering quickly is therefore not about pride but about accuracy. It also matters for the people we serve: a rumour that a distribution has stopped will keep families at home, and some of them will not come back. For example, when a message said our sites had closed, we published the real position within two hours, and attendance the next day was normal.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear opinion?  ☐ two or three reasons?  ☐ one example?  ☐ 80–120 words?


### Part 6: Reflection — A Steady Voice (60–90 words)
**Write about staying calm in a crisis. Use your own ideas.**

**Model — read this first:**

> What I have learned is that people are not really asking for information in the first hour; they are asking whether anybody is in control. A short, honest statement answers that question even when it contains almost no facts. I used to want to wait until I had the full picture, and waiting made everything worse. Now I say what I know, say what I do not, and promise a time. The promise matters more than the content.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear main idea?  ☐ reasons or examples?  ☐ 60–90 words?

### Part 8: Reading — The Rumour and the Update
*Before you read: how fast does a rumour travel where you work?*

> It began on a Tuesday evening with a message in a community group: the food distribution in the north had stopped. It was not true, and it was not malicious. Somebody had walked to the third site, found it closed because the road had flooded that morning, and told their neighbours what they had seen. By Wednesday at eight, Joseph had been calling the districts for an hour and had confirmed that two of the three sites were open as normal. By nine, the message had reached four thousand phones. Nadia, who had been watching the channels since seven, said something that changed how the team now works: the problem was not the rumour, which was a reasonable conclusion from what one person had seen. The problem was that the team had known about the flooded road on Tuesday morning and had not thought it worth announcing. The update went out at ten, and it led with what was true rather than with the rumour. It also said, in one sentence, that the organisation should have announced the closure on Tuesday and was sorry. Attendance on Thursday was normal. The team now publishes every site closure on the day it happens, however small, and the habit has prevented three similar rumours since.

## Part 9  ·  Decision Task
*[OP] Officer track  ·  judgement*


### Part 9: Fast or Confirmed?
*Before you read: would you publish something useful that you have not yet confirmed?*

> At seven in the morning in Amman, Layla has a problem that will not wait. An earthquake overnight has damaged a road, and families in two villages are asking on social media whether tomorrow’s mobile clinic will come. Layla has been on the phone since five. The district team believes the clinic can reach the first village by a longer route but is not certain, and will not be certain until the driver attempts it at eleven. If Layla publishes now that the clinic will come, and it cannot, people will walk for two hours for nothing, some of them with children and some of them unwell. If she publishes that it will not come, and it could have, those same people will stay at home unnecessarily. If she says nothing until eleven, four hours of silence will fill with guesses, and some of those guesses will be worse than either answer. The organisation’s rule is clear that she must not publish an unverified fact. The rule says nothing about what to publish instead.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

0. What has damaged the road? — An earthquake overnight.

1. When will the district team be certain?
2. What happens if Layla publishes that the clinic will come and it cannot?
3. What does the rule not say?


### Part 9: Make the Decision
**Should Layla (a) publish that the clinic will come, (b) publish that it will not, or (c) publish what she knows and promise an update at eleven? Choose one and give reasons.**

**Answer frame:** ‘I think Layla should ___ , because ___ . Also, ___ . This is better than ___ , because ___ .’

**Model — read this first:**

> Model decision: I think Layla should publish what she knows and promise an update at eleven, because she can be completely honest without guessing: the road is damaged, a longer route is being attempted, and we will know by eleven. Also, that message lets a family decide for itself whether to set out, which is their decision and not ours. This is better than announcing either answer, because both would be a guess dressed as a fact, and better than silence, because four hours of silence will fill with worse guesses than the truth.

**Phrase bank:** I think… should…  ·  because…  ·  honest without guessing  ·  This is better than…  ·  a guess dressed as a fact.

### Warm-up: Reading — A Quote Is a Promise
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> A quote is a promise. When Meridian Relief puts a sentence inside quotation marks, it is promising the reader that the person said exactly those words, and promising the speaker that their words will not be improved, shortened into something sharper, or moved into a context they never agreed to. If a sentence needs tidying, the team paraphrases it and drops the quotation marks. If a speaker asks for a word to be changed after a read-back, the word is changed. And every claim carries attribution, so that a reader can see who said it and decide what to think.

- ○ D) Publish it anyway

**2. Why does every claim carry attribution?**

## Part 2  ·  Grammar — Reported Speech
*[OP] Officer track  ·  grammar focus*


### Part 2: Notice
> Read Tomás’s note after the meeting. ‘Mrs Dela Cruz said that the market opened at five and that she had been going there for eleven years. She told me that she did not want her children mentioned. She asked whether the article would appear in English only, and she asked me to send her a copy. I said that I would call her when it was published.’ Notice what happens: the verbs step back one tense, ‘tomorrow’ becomes ‘the next day’, and a question becomes a statement with ‘whether’ or ‘if’.

**Look at the sentences again. What did each person actually say?**


### Part 2: Grammar Focus Box

|  | Direct | Reported | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Statement | ‘I work here.’ | She said that she worked there. |  |
| Present perfect | ‘We have finished.’ | He said that they had finished. |  |
| Question | ‘Have you finished?’ | She asked whether we had finished. |  |
| Command | ‘Do not publish my name.’ | He asked us not to publish his name. |  |

**Remember:** The verb usually steps back one tense: present → past, present perfect → past perfect, will → would, can → could. ‘Say’ takes no person; ‘tell’ takes one: she told me.

**Watch out!** Watch out: in a reported question there is no inversion and no question mark. Say ‘She asked whether we had finished’, not ‘She asked had we finished?’.

**Gloss:** inversion = putting the verb before the subject, as in a question    ·    reporting verb = a verb like say, tell, ask or explain

## Part 3  ·  Listening and Dialogue
*[OP] Officer track  ·  listening*


### Part 3: Ingrid Explains Reporting Speech
**🔊 Audio Track 10.2**

*Before you listen: when is it better to quote somebody, and when is it better to paraphrase?*

> Ingrid: There are two honest ways to use what somebody says. You quote them word for word, inside quotation marks. Or you report them in your own words, with attribution and no marks. What you may never do is the thing in between: tidy a sentence and then put marks around it. That is not a quote; it is your sentence wearing somebody else’s name. So when should you quote? When the words carry something — a way of putting it you could not improve, or a judgement that must clearly be theirs. When should you report? When the information matters more than the phrasing, or when the speaker was tired, or speaking through an interpreter, or simply not making a speech. And always attribute. A reader who sees ‘Mrs Dela Cruz said’ can decide what to think. A reader who sees a claim with no name has to trust us, and we should not ask for that when we do not need to.

*While you listen: write True (T) or False (F). (0. is done.)*

0. There are two honest ways to use what somebody says. — T

1. A quote must be word for word.   ____
2. It is acceptable to tidy a sentence inside quotation marks.   ____
3. You should report rather than quote when the information matters more than the phrasing.   ____
4. A claim with no attribution is better for the reader.   ____

**Useful phrases:** word for word, inside quotation marks  ·  your sentence wearing somebody else’s name  ·  always attribute

## Part 5  ·  Extended Reading
*[OP] Officer track  ·  extended reading*


### Part 5: Telling the Story Truthfully
**Read the text and choose the correct answer.**

> There are two honest ways to use what somebody has told you, and one dishonest one that is extremely common. The honest ways are to quote them word for word inside quotation marks, or to report them in your own words with attribution. The dishonest way is the thing in between: taking a sentence that was slightly rambling, tidying it, sharpening it, and then putting quotation marks around the improved version. Almost everybody who does it believes they are helping, and almost everybody it is done to notices. A quote is not a service to the reader; it is a promise that these were the words. Attribution is the second half of the same promise. A reader who sees ‘Mrs Dela Cruz said’ can weigh the claim against the person who made it; a reader who sees the same claim floating free has to trust the organisation instead, and an organisation that asks for that trust unnecessarily will eventually spend it on something that matters. There is a further problem in international work. A quote that has passed through an interpreter is not verbatim in the language it is printed in. Honest teams say ‘speaking through an interpreter’, read the final version back in the original language, and accept the changes the speaker asks for. The result is less polished than an invented sentence would be. It is also the only version the speaker would recognise as theirs.

0. There are two honest ways to use what somebody has told you. (example)

**1. What is the dishonest way described?**
- ○ A) Quoting word for word
- ○ B) Tidying a sentence and keeping the quotation marks
- ○ C) Paraphrasing with attribution
- ○ D) Not quoting at all

**2. What can a reader do when they see attribution?**
- ○ A) Nothing
- ○ B) Weigh the claim against the person
- ○ C) Translate it
- ○ D) Share it faster

**3. What do honest teams do with an interpreted quote?**
- ○ A) Print it as verbatim
- ○ B) Say ‘speaking through an interpreter’ and read it back
- ○ C) Remove it
- ○ D) Shorten it

### Part 5: Whose Words Are They?
**Read about quotes across languages. Then mark each sentence True (T) or False (F).**

> Almost every organisation that works internationally publishes quotes that were not spoken in the language they appear in, and most of them say nothing about it. The sentence looks the same on the page as one spoken in English, and the reader assumes the speaker chose those words. They did not. Somebody chose words with the same meaning, as carefully as they could, under time pressure and usually without a chance to check. This is not dishonest in itself, and the alternative — publishing nothing that was said in another language — would silence most of the people whose stories matter. What is dishonest is hiding it. Three habits fix almost all of it. Write ‘speaking through an interpreter’ where it is true, so that the reader knows what they are reading. Read the final version back in the original language before publication, not the interpreter’s notes but the sentence that will actually be printed. And when the speaker says that a word is not quite right, change it, even when the change makes the sentence flatter. A flatter sentence that the speaker would recognise is worth more than a beautiful one that they would not.

0. Many published quotes were not spoken in the language they appear in. → T (example)

1. Publishing an interpreted quote is dishonest in itself.   ____
2. ‘Speaking through an interpreter’ should be written where it is true.   ____
3. The interpreter’s notes should be read back, not the final sentence.   ____
4. A flatter sentence the speaker recognises is worth more than a beautiful one.   ____

### Part 6: Why We Never Invent a Quote (80–120 words)
**Write about why a quote must never be invented or improved. Give reasons and an example.**

**Model — read this first:**

> An invented quote is the one mistake from which an organisation does not recover. Everything else we publish — a figure, a date, a caption — can be corrected, and a reader will accept a correction. A quote cannot be corrected, because the person either said it or did not, and if they did not, every other quote we have ever printed becomes a question. Improving a quote is the same offence in a smaller coat. For example, a sentence that was rambling can be paraphrased honestly with attribution; what it cannot be is tidied and then put inside quotation marks.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear opinion?  ☐ two or three reasons?  ☐ one example?  ☐ 80–120 words?

**Write about what you have learned in this course. Use your own ideas.**

**Model — read this first:**

> What I take from this course is that being allowed to tell somebody’s story is a privilege, not a right. People give us their words when they have very little else to give, and they usually cannot check what we do with them afterwards. That is why consent, accuracy, dignity and do no harm are not rules imposed on the work; they are the work. If I remember nothing else, I want to remember to read it back.

**Check before you finish:** ☐ a clear main idea?  ☐ reasons or examples?  ☐ 60–90 words?

### 7B: The End-of-Course Briefing
**🔊 Audio Track 10.5**

*Before you listen: what would you want a new colleague to remember after a year?*

> Ingrid: We have been working together for ten units now, and I want to say what I hope you take away, because it is not the grammar. Four things. Consent: never use a person’s words, face or story without permission, and remember that permission is specific to a use. Accuracy: check every fact and every quote, and never invent anything, not even a small helpful detail. Dignity: treat every person in your work with respect, and protect those who could be at risk — a photograph that takes somebody’s dignity is a photograph we do not need. And do no harm: if something could hurt somebody, do not publish it, whatever it would do for the campaign. Everything else in this book is technique, and technique can be learned in a month. These four take longer, and they are the reason that people trust us with the things they tell us. Thank you for your work. I have enjoyed it more than I expected to.

## Part 8  ·  Consolidation

### Part 8: Reading — The Quote That Was Almost Wrong
*Before you read: has a small change of wording ever changed a meaning for you?*

> The article was about a women’s cooperative in Lima, and the quote was the best sentence in it. A member of the cooperative had said, through an interpreter, something that came out in the notes as: ‘Before, we asked our husbands for money. Now we do not have to ask anybody.’ It was clear, it was quotable, and Nadia had already chosen it for the social media card. Tomás, following the rule rather than any suspicion, asked Joseph to read the final English sentence back in Spanish before publication. The woman listened and said that it was nearly right but not quite. She had not said ‘we do not have to ask anybody’. She had said that she no longer had to ask for money to buy materials for her work, which was a smaller and more precise claim about her business rather than a general statement about her marriage. The interpreter had not made an error exactly; the Spanish had been compressed, and the English had filled the gap in the direction that made the better sentence. The published quote was the smaller one. The social media card was less striking. Tomás wrote afterwards that the read-back had taken eleven minutes and had saved them from putting a sentence about somebody’s marriage into her mouth in a language she does not read.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

1. What did the notes say she had said?
2. What had she actually said?
3. How long did the read-back take?

## Part 9  ·  Decision Task
*[OP] Officer track  ·  judgement*


### Part 9: The Donor’s Own Words
*Before you read: should a donor’s words be checked as carefully as anybody else’s?*

> A donor who has funded the Lima programme for six years has sent a message that Nadia would like to use in the annual report. It reads: ‘I have visited the cooperative twice, and I have never seen money better spent.’ It is warm, it is specific, and it is exactly the kind of endorsement that persuades other donors. There are two problems. The donor wrote it in an email that was not intended for publication, and she has not been asked. And Tomás, checking the record as he checks everything, has found that she visited once, not twice; the second visit was cancelled when the road flooded. The sentence is therefore not accurate, although the inaccuracy is the donor’s own and is obviously innocent. Nadia could simply ask the donor, who would almost certainly agree and would correct the detail herself. That would take three days, and the report goes to the printer on Thursday. She could also use the quote without the word ‘twice’, which would be accurate and would no longer be verbatim.

**Answer the questions. (0. is done.)**

0. How long has the donor funded the programme? — Six years.

1. What are the two problems with the quote?
2. How many times did the donor actually visit?
3. What would happen if Nadia simply asked her?


### Part 9: Make the Decision
**Should Nadia (a) use the quote as written, (b) use it without the word ‘twice’, or (c) ask the donor and delay? Choose one and give reasons.**

**Answer frame:** ‘I think Nadia should ___ , because ___ . Also, ___ . This is better than ___ , because ___ .’

**Model — read this first:**

> Model decision: I think Nadia should ask the donor and accept the delay, because the quote was written in a private email and we have not been given permission to publish it at all, which is the larger problem. Also, the donor will almost certainly agree and will want to correct the detail herself, since it is her own mistake and her own reputation. This is better than quietly removing a word, because an edited quote inside quotation marks is no longer verbatim, and we would be doing to a donor exactly what we would never do to anybody else.

**Phrase bank:** I think… should…  ·  because…  ·  it was written in a private email  ·  This is better than…  ·  the same rule for everybody.

My decision: ______  because ______ .

### Part 10: End of Course — The Four Values
**You have reached the end of the course. Everything in this book rests on four simple values. Keep them with you.**

> Consent — never use a person’s words, face or story without permission, and remember that permission is specific to a use.  ·  Accuracy — check every fact and every quote, and never invent anything.  ·  Dignity — treat every person with respect, and protect those who could be at risk.  ·  Do no harm — if something could hurt someone, do not publish it.

Well done for completing the course. You have learned how to write, interview, plan, report and protect, in a team that works across several countries and several languages. Carry these skills, and these values, into everything you communicate. Congratulations.


### Part 10: Unit 10 glossary
> quote = a person’s exact words    ·    attribution = saying clearly who said something    ·    report = to tell what someone said, in your own words    ·    donor = a person who gives money to help    ·    credit = naming the person who did the work    ·    paraphrase = to say something again in different words    ·    source = the person or place information comes from    ·    acknowledge = to thank or give credit to someone    ·    verbatim = in exactly the same words    ·    anonymous = without the person’s name    ·    endorsement = a public statement of support    ·    reported speech = telling what someone said in your own words    ·    reporting verb = a verb like say, tell, ask or explain    ·    privilege = a special honour or opportunity    ·    cooperative = a business owned and run by its members together    ·    communicator = a person whose job is to share information and stories
